My family has farmed this land in Quzhou for generations. I know one thing well: wheat in winter, corn in summer. Everyone in the village does it this way, and the soil here on the North China Plain is made for it. I have about 15 mu of flat, irrigated land. There is no reason to try anything different — I need reliable income, and these two crops I know how to grow.

For wheat, I will go to the seed shop in the county town and buy what the shopkeeper says is selling well this year. Last year my neighbor used Jimai 22 and it did fine. I will plant all 15 mu in October. I always apply base fertilizer at planting — a bag of diammonium phosphate and urea. Then in spring before jointing I top-dress more urea. I learned this from my father. I will irrigate three times: once in November before the ground freezes, once at jointing in April, once before heading in May. I spray herbicide in the seedling stage and sometimes a fungicide if I see rust on the leaves. I use rotary tillage — I rent the machine from the village.

For corn, right after wheat harvest in June I rotary-till and drill in hybrid seed — Zhengdan 958 or whatever they have. Everyone uses hybrid corn now. I apply compound fertilizer at planting and top-dress urea when the corn reaches knee height. Summer rains usually help, but I pump groundwater once or twice if it is dry in August. I spray herbicide right after planting and watch for pests, but usually one spray is enough.

I expect around 450 jin of wheat and 550-600 jin of corn per mu. Not record yields, but steady. That is what matters at my age.
